title: "The Enemy Is at Honnō-ji": Who Really Wrote Mitsuhide's Famous Line?
description:
The night of the 1st day of the 6th month, Tenshō 10 (June 20, 1582, Julian): Akechi Mitsuhide's army left Kameyama Castle, turned left at the fork on Mount Oino and headed for Kyoto. Every story today says he shouted "The enemy is at Honnō-ji!" But who first wrote that line down?

This episode follows the line in the order the records appeared. In the Shinchō Kōki, Nobunaga's scribe Ōta Gyūichi has Mitsuhide tell the army they will march "via Yamazaki to Settsu." Luís Fróis reports the soldiers were told Nobunaga wanted to review them, and some thought the target was Ieyasu. In Kan'ei 17 (1640), Honjō Sōemon, who marched that night, wrote "we only thought it was Ieyasu." The Kawasumi Taikōki has Saitō Toshimitsu send the units toward the trees of Honnō-ji. None of them has the line.

The earliest we have found is the Oda Nobunaga Fu by Hayashi Razan and his son, presented to the shogun in Kan'ei 18 (1641); we read the Kyoto print of Meireki 4 (1658), not the presented copy. There a soldier asks at Ōeyama and Mitsuhide answers "The enemy is at Honnō-ji." Rai San'yō's Nihon Gaishi (sent to Matsudaira Sadanobu in Bunsei 10, 1827) moves the scene to the Katsura River, with Mitsuhide raising his whip and declaring "My enemy is at Honnō-ji." Its bibliography lists the Oda Nobunaga Fu, which already has the self-defense motive and the council of five.

Fróis and the Kawasumi Taikōki are read as quoted by Tokutomi Sohō, and Honjō's memoir from a Wikipedia transcription; we did not open those originals. "Earliest" means as far as we have searched. Why Mitsuhide rose is still unsettled: this episode closes the case of the line, not the motive.

Sources for every quotation, year and number are in the references below. Narration dates use the old lunar calendar. Sentences beginning "we think" are this channel's view.

Illustrations are AI-generated; historical figures are unnamed cartoon characters, not likenesses. Tokutomi Sohō and modern researchers are not drawn, and events inside Honnō-ji are not shown.

Information as of 2026-10-20

chapters.slim-book: Kan'ei 18: a book for the shogun

hn102.text: Akechi Mitsuhide and 10,000-plus men leave Kameyama Castle.

hn103.text: Instead of heading west, they turn east, up Mount Oino.

hn104.text: On the mountain the road forks: right to Yamazaki and Settsu; left, down to Kyoto.

hn106.text: Today every story says he shouted: "The enemy is at Honnō-ji!"

hn107.text: But is that what the soldiers heard?

hn108.text: Nobunaga's scribe recorded Mitsuhide's order to the army.

hn109.text: 58 years later, a veteran of that night wrote what he thought the target was.

hn110.text: In Kan'ei 18, a shogunate Confucian gave a book to the shogun.

hn111.text: In Bunsei 10, a history 20-plus years in the making reached Matsudaira Sadanobu.

hn112.text: "The enemy is at Honnō-ji": who wrote it first?

hn201.text: The first to write that night down was Nobunaga's scribe, Ōta Gyūichi.

hn202.text: His Shinchō Kōki is the era's most detailed record; but that night, he wasn't there.

hn203.text: It says that night Mitsuhide consulted only four senior retainers: kill Nobunaga, rule the realm.

hn205.text: What he told the soldiers: via Yamazaki, march on Settsu.

hn206.text: In the whole volume, that's all he says to them.

hn208.text: Four months later, Hideyoshi's man of letters Ōmura Yūko wrote an account too;

hn209.text: it only says Mitsuhide set out from Kameyama. No announcement at all.

hn210.text: Missionary Luís Fróis's report to the Church differs again; we read Tokutomi Sohō's translation.

hn211.text: Mitsuhide said: Nobunaga wants to review our troops.

hn212.text: But in the ranks, some wondered: secret orders to go after Ieyasu?

hn213.text: And what did a man in the column say?

hn214.text: The veteran from the start was Honjō Sōemon; in Kan'ei 17, he wrote that night down.

hn216.text: He wrote: we thought we were bound for Yamazaki, but we were told Kyoto.

hn217.text: Lord Ieyasu was in the capital then; we only thought it was Ieyasu.

hn218.text: He adds: Honnō-ji? I didn't even know where it was.

hn219.text: So how did he get there?

hn220.text: He followed Saitō Toshimitsu's son; Toshimitsu was one of the four that night.

hn221.text: Crossing the Katsura, dawn was near.

hn222.text: The next moment is in an earlier book: the Kawasumi Taikōki, from around the 1620s.

hn223.text: Tokutomi Sohō says it records officers' own experience.

hn224.text: Near Kyoto, Toshimitsu ordered: open the ward gates, units split up.

hn227.text: Only at Kyoto's edge was Honnō-ji pointed out; no "enemy" there, and not from Mitsuhide.

hn228.text: Nobunaga was staying at Honnō-ji, with only 20 or 30 attendants.

hn230.text: That day, Tenshō 10, 6th month, 2nd day, Nobunaga died in the temple.

hn231.text: No record we read has this line; so who first put it in a book?

hn301.text: The earliest found so far: that book given to the shogun in Kan'ei 18, the Oda Nobunaga Fu.

hn302.text: Its end says: by the shogun's order, begun early month 11, presented month 12, day 7.

hn303.text: 59 years after that night, and a year after the veteran's memoir.

hn304.text: It's signed by shogunate scholar Hayashi Razan, noting: drafted by his son Shunsai.

hn305.text: It calls Ieyasu "Daigongen": a father and son writing Oda history for the Tokugawa.

hn306.text: Sadly, we haven't seen the copy given to the shogun;

hn307.text: we read the Kyoto print of Meireki 4, 17 years later.

hn308.text: How does it tell that night?

hn309.text: Here the omen comes earlier: at a renga gathering before the march, Mitsuhide asks: how deep is Honnō-ji's moat?

hn310.text: He eats chimaki, leaves and all.

hn311.text: Neither is in the Shinchō Kōki's renga gathering.

hn312.text: Then, at Kameyama Castle, Mitsuhide secretly summons retainers. The Shinchō Kōki had four; now, five.

hn314.text: He asks: will you die for me? If not, cut off my head.

hn315.text: Then he gives his reason: Nobunaga means to kill me.

hn316.text: Marching at once, he orders: into the capital tomorrow, to show Nobunaga our troops.

hn317.text: The review the missionary heard of is here too.

hn318.text: At Ōeyama, the puzzled soldiers ask: where are we going?

hn321.text: Only then did they see he was rebelling.

hn322.text: 180-some years later, the scene was written again.

hn401.text: By the history from the start, sent to Matsudaira Sadanobu: Rai San'yō's Nihon Gaishi.

hn402.text: His letter to Sadanobu is dated Bunsei 10, 5th month: the book sat unshown in a box; Sadanobu sent for it.

hn403.text: Is his night the same as the Hayashis'?

hn404.text: His pretext is new: not a review, but orders to go west and support Hideyoshi.

hn405.text: By night he crossed Ōeyama to Oinosaka.

hn406.text: Remember the fork? This book says: right is the road to Bitchū.

hn407.text: He went left; his soldiers were stunned.

hn409.text: No one asked. The column crossed the Katsura.

hn410.text: Mitsuhide raised his whip, pointed east, and declared:

hn411.text: "Waga teki wa Honnō-ji ni ari": my enemy is at Honnō-ji.

hn412.text: The renga line, "How deep is Honnō-ji's moat?", is here too.

hn413.text: Even "only then did they see he was rebelling" nearly matches the Oda Nobunaga Fu.

hn415.text: Remember the 1641 book? It put the line at Ōeyama; here, it moves to the Katsura.

hn416.text: The line went from an answer to a declaration.

hn417.text: It also gained "my" and an emphatic ending.

hn418.text: But is there a thread between the two books?

hn419.text: The Nihon Gaishi's bibliography lists the Oda Nobunaga Fu.

hn420.text: In it, Mitsuhide also asks if his men will die for him, and says: Nobunaga nearly killed me often.

hn421.text: "Nobunaga means to kill me" is already in the Oda Nobunaga Fu; Rai San'yō didn't invent the self-defense motive.

hn423.text: We think that scene is what a line needs to become famous.

hn424.text: The Nihon Gaishi became the most-read history from the late Edo era to Meiji.

hn425.text: So where did Mitsuhide's whip-raised line end up?

hn501.text: In everyday Japanese: by Meiji 28, a book was already using it as an idiom,

hn502.text: meaning: the real target lies elsewhere.

hn503.text: Meiji textbooks and popular histories kept both: some ask and answer, some raise the whip.

hn504.text: We find it fitting: the line's real author, too, lies elsewhere.

hn505.text: So who wrote "The enemy is at Honnō-ji"?

hn506.text: It's a later line; the earliest we've found to write it: Hayashi Razan and son.

hn507.text: As for why Mitsuhide rose—grudge, ambition, Shikoku politics—someone sorted the theories into 50 kinds;

hn508.text: to this day, none is settled.

hn509.text: So the line's case: filed. The motive's case: still open.

hn510.text: Where did you first hear this line?

hn511.text: We tell only what records show. Subscribe to open the files with us.
